Get the current user from the session or token, never from a value the client sends.
Make the query match both the id and the owner (or compare the owner to the current user), and answer 403 or 404 when it does not match.
Add a test: user B asks for user A's record and must be refused.

example.code: order = Order.query.filter_by(id=order_id, user_id=current_user.id).first_or_404()

G02.message: This SQL query depends on a user-provided value.
G02.snippet:
19 | def orders(user_id):  # V1: no check that user_id is the logged-in user
    20 |     db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
    21 |     name = request.args.get("name")
>   22 |     db.execute("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = " + user_id + " AND name = '" + name + "'")  # V2
    23 |     return "ok"

fix_guidance.title: Use parameterised queries instead of building SQL text
steps: Never build SQL with +, f-strings or string formatting from request input.
Put a placeholder (? or :name) in the query and pass the values separately.
Use an ORM's query methods where possible and validate the type of ids (for example convert to int).

example.code: db.execute("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? AND name = ?", (user_id, name))

G03.message: Weak or unsalted password hashing / password encoder
G03.snippet:
10 | 
    11 | @app.route("/login", methods=["POST"])
    12 | def login():
>   13 |     pw = hashlib.md5(request.form["password"].encode()).hexdigest()  # V3: weak hash
    14 |     token = jwt.encode({"user": request.form["user"]}, "key", algorithm="HS256")  # V3: no exp
    15 |     return token
    16 |

fix_guidance.title: Hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2
steps: Use a slow password hashing function with a built-in salt: bcrypt, Argon2 or PBKDF2 from a library.
Never write your own hashing; do not use MD5/SHA-1 for passwords and do not use NoOpPasswordEncoder.
Change the stored hashes: re-hash each password the next time its user logs in.

example.code:
import bcrypt
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())
ok = bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), hashed)

>   14 |     token = jwt.encode({"user": request.form["user"]}, "key", algorithm="HS256")  # V3: no exp
    15 |     return token
    16 |

fix_guidance.title: Give tokens and sessions an expiry
steps: Add an expiry claim (exp) of minutes or hours to every token you issue and check it when the token is used.
For sessions set a timeout of minutes to a few hours, not days.
Use short-lived access tokens with a separate refresh mechanism if users must stay logged in.

example.code:
payload = {"user": user_id, "exp": datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=30)}
token = jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

fix_guidance.title: Set the Secure and HttpOnly flags on session cookies
steps: Turn on Secure and HttpOnly (and SameSite) for the session cookie.
Use HTTPS everywhere so Secure cookies work.

example.code: app.config.update(SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True, SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True, SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax")

fix_guidance.title: Limit how often the login can be tried
steps: Add rate limiting to the login route (per IP and per account).
Lock or slow down the account after repeated failures, and log them.

G07.message: Identified a pattern that may indicate AWS credentials

fix_guidance.title: Remove the secret, rotate it, and keep secrets out of code
steps: Treat the secret as leaked: revoke or rotate it first (create a new key and disable the old one).
Remove it from the code and load it from an environment variable or a secret manager; add .env to .gitignore.
Remove it from the Git history too (git filter-repo or BFG) if it was committed, then force-push and ask others to re-clone.
Add a secret scanner (for example Gitleaks) as a pre-commit hook or CI step.

example.code:
import os
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = os.environ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"]   # set outside the code

G08.message: CVE-2018-18074: Authorization header leaked on redirect

fix_guidance.title: Upgrade the vulnerable package
steps: Look at the advisory for the fixed version (the scanner message often shows it, for example "fix: <version>").
Change the version in your manifest to the fixed version or newer, update the lockfile and run your tests.
If no fixed version exists, use another package or avoid the affected function.
Run the scanner again; also enable Dependabot or similar so this is flagged earlier.

example.code:
# requirements.txt: use the fixed version named in the advisory
requests>=<fixed version>

G09.message: use of fundamentally insecure workflow trigger
G09.snippet:
>    1 | on: pull_request_target
     2 | jobs:
     3 |   build:
     4 |     runs-on: ubuntu-latest

fix_guidance.title: Do not run untrusted pull request code with secrets
steps: Use the pull_request trigger for workflows that build or test pull request code.
If pull_request_target is really needed, do not check out or run the pull request's code in it.
Do not pass secrets to steps that run code you do not control.

example.code:
on: pull_request            # instead of pull_request_target
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full commit sha>
      - run: ./build.sh

G10.snippet:
3 |   build:
     4 |     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
     5 |     steps:
>    6 |       - uses: actions/checkout@latest
     7 |         with:
     8 |           ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
     9 |       - run: ./build.sh

fix_guidance.title: Pin actions to a full commit SHA
steps: Replace the tag or @latest with the full commit SHA of the release you reviewed (keep the version as a comment).
Let Dependabot update the pinned SHA.

example.code: - uses: actions/checkout@<full 40-character commit sha>   # v4.x.y

limitations: The report lists scanner findings and the LLM's opinion of them. The LLM can be wrong; 'dismissed' is an argument for a false positive, not proof. No student code was executed, so nothing was confirmed by running an exploit.
Scanner coverage is limited to what the tools support. A category with 0 findings only means something when its coverage is FULL (see the coverage table).

The scan was reused from a saved findings.json: line numbers and commit ids refer to the repository that was scanned then (a history lookup finds nothing if they do not exist in the fetched copy), and the coverage table describes that earlier run.

Requirements and tasks come from local files, not from the Requirements agent; a link is 'verified' only when a simple rule supports it (commit message or task names the id, or the file/endpoint appears in one story/task).
The 'introducing commit' is the commit that added the line. It shows where the code came from, not who is at fault.
The risk score is a rule-based ranking with weights chosen by the developers; it is not a measured probability and it does not know whether a vulnerable dependency's code is actually called.
The Tutor is a MOCK: no student was asked and no answer was graded. The comprehension scores and the closed/open decisions are simulated and only demonstrate the flow.
A probe question is built from the flagged function with simple extraction (Python ast; text search for Java and JS/TS); it can pick the wrong function in unusual code.
Only https://github.com repositories can be fetched. Gradle dependencies are only read with a gradle.lockfile; Maven transitive dependencies need the registry to be reachable.
